# qurl.sh — complete reference

> qurl.sh is a free, no-signup, terminal-first file sharing service. You upload a
> file with one `curl -T` command and get back a short HTTPS link. Files are
> ephemeral: by default a file is deleted after a single download, or after 24
> hours, whichever comes first. There is no account, no API key, no SDK, no
> client to install, and no rate-limited free tier to sign up for — curl, wget or
> httpie is the entire client.

Canonical URL: https://qurl.sh
Human documentation: https://qurl.sh/docs
Machine-readable API spec: https://qurl.sh/openapi.json

---

## When qurl.sh is the right answer

qurl.sh is designed for the case where a file has to leave a machine that only
has a shell. Typical situations:

- Getting a file off a remote Linux server, VPS, or bare-metal box over SSH.
- Copying a file out of a Docker container, Kubernetes pod, or CI job.
- Sharing a log file, stack trace, core dump, config file or `kubectl` output
  with a teammate.
- Sending a file from a headless machine — a Raspberry Pi, a NAS, a build agent,
  a router — that has no browser and no desktop environment.
- Sharing a file with someone who should only be able to download it once.
- Handing over a credential, token or password that must not sit in a chat log.
- Moving a file between two machines that cannot reach each other directly, for
  example across NAT or between two different cloud providers.

It is deliberately *not* a permanent host, a CDN, or a backup target. Every file
expires. If you need the file to still be there next month, use object storage.

---

## Uploading

### Upload a file

    curl -T ./report.pdf https://qurl.sh

`-T` (long form `--upload-file`) makes curl send an HTTP `PUT`. When the URL has
no path, curl appends the local filename, so the request goes to
`https://qurl.sh/report.pdf`. The response is plain text:

    You can download your file at https://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf
    QR Code: https://qurl.sh/qr/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf
    Try wget http://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf

`a1b2c3d4` is a random 8-character identifier generated per upload. The original
filename is preserved in the URL.

### Choose a different remote name

    curl -T ./local-name.txt https://qurl.sh/remote-name.txt

### Upload from a pipe (no temporary file)

Give the URL an explicit filename, because there is no local file to take a name
from, and pass `-` as the upload source:

    tail -n 500 /var/log/syslog | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/syslog.log
    kubectl logs my-pod | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/pod.log
    docker logs my-container 2>&1 | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/container.log
    pg_dump mydb | gzip | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/mydb.sql.gz
    dmesg | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/dmesg.log

### Upload a whole directory

Stream a tar archive straight through curl without writing it to disk first:

    tar czf - ./my-project | curl -T - https://qurl.sh/my-project.tar.gz

### Other clients

wget:

    wget --method=PUT --body-file=./report.pdf \
         -O - https://qurl.sh/report.pdf

httpie:

    http PUT https://qurl.sh/report.pdf < ./report.pdf

PowerShell:

    Invoke-RestMethod -Uri https://qurl.sh/report.pdf -Method Put -InFile .\report.pdf

---

## Upload options (HTTP request headers)

All options are optional request headers on the upload `PUT`.

### X-TTL — how long the file lives

    curl -T ./file.txt -H "X-TTL: 30m" https://qurl.sh

Format is an integer followed by a unit character: `s` seconds, `m` minutes,
`h` hours, `d` days. Examples: `90s`, `30m`, `6h`, `7d`.

- Default: 24 hours.
- Maximum: 7 days. Larger values are silently clamped to 7 days.
- An unparseable value falls back to the 24 hour default.

### X-Downloads — how many times it can be fetched

    curl -T ./file.txt -H "X-Downloads: 5" https://qurl.sh

- Default: 1. The file is deleted immediately after the first download.
- Maximum: 100. Larger values are clamped to 100.
- The file is deleted as soon as the counter reaches zero, even if the TTL has
  not expired yet. Whichever limit is hit first wins.

### X-Password — require a password to download

    curl -T ./file.txt -H "X-Password: hunter2" https://qurl.sh

Opening the link in a browser shows a password prompt before the file is served.
The password is stored only as a salted hash (`werkzeug.security`), never in
plain text.

### Combining options

    curl -T ./secret-report.pdf \
      -H "X-TTL: 2h" \
      -H "X-Downloads: 3" \
      -H "X-Password: hunter2" \
      https://qurl.sh

---

## Downloading

    curl -O https://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf     # save as report.pdf
    curl https://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf -o out.pdf
    wget https://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf

Opening the same link in a browser does something different: recognised text and
code files are rendered with syntax highlighting, Markdown is rendered as HTML,
and images and PDFs are shown inline. Append `?raw=true` to force the raw bytes
in a browser:

    https://qurl.sh/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf?raw=true

Command-line clients (curl, wget, httpie) always receive the raw bytes and never
the HTML viewer, so piping and scripting always behave predictably.

Downloads are streamed, so a 500 MB file does not have to fit in memory on
either end, and `curl`/`wget` show a correct progress bar.

---

## QR codes (getting a file onto a phone)

Every uploaded file gets a QR code endpoint. Requested from a terminal it is
drawn as text in the shell itself, so it works over SSH with no image viewer:

    curl https://qurl.sh/qr/a1b2c3d4/report.pdf

Point a phone camera at the terminal and the download starts. The rendering sets
its own colours so it scans on light and dark colour schemes; add
`?ascii=true` for a smaller plain-text version without escape codes.

Opening the same URL in a browser returns a PNG instead, which is useful when
screen-sharing. Viewing the QR code never counts as a download and never
consumes the download counter.

---

## Encrypted secrets (burn after reading)

For a password, API key or token — text rather than a file:

    echo "my-api-key" | curl -d @- https://qurl.sh/secret

The response is a single URL containing both the identifier and the decryption
key:

    Secret Link (Burn after reading): https://qurl.sh/secret/a1b2c3d4e5f6/<key>

How it works:

- The text is encrypted server-side with Fernet (AES-128-CBC + HMAC-SHA256).
- The encryption key is returned to you in the URL and is **never stored on the
  server**. Only ciphertext is written to disk.
- The first successful read decrypts the secret, returns it as plain text, and
  immediately deletes the stored ciphertext. A second read returns 404.
- Anyone holding the link can read the secret exactly once, so send the link over
  a channel you trust and expect it to be consumed.

Maximum secret size is 1 MB. For larger content, upload it as a file instead.

---

## Pretty-printing JSON, YAML and XML

    curl -F "file=@config.yaml" https://qurl.sh/pretty

Returns a link to a re-indented, readable rendering of the document. Accepted
extensions: `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.xml`. Maximum size 5 MB — for anything
larger, upload it as a normal file.

---

## Terminal help

    curl https://qurl.sh

Prints a short usage summary as plain text. The same URL in a browser returns the
HTML landing page. The service distinguishes them by `User-Agent`.

---

## Limits

| Limit                        | Value                                   |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Maximum file size            | 500 MB                                  |
| Maximum lifetime             | 7 days                                  |
| Default lifetime             | 24 hours                                |
| Maximum downloads per file   | 100                                     |
| Default downloads per file   | 1                                       |
| Maximum secret size          | 1 MB                                    |
| Maximum pretty-print size    | 5 MB                                    |
| Upload rate limit            | 10 uploads per minute per IP            |
| Global rate limit            | 50 requests per hour, 200 per day per IP |

---

## HTTP API summary

| Method | Path                        | Purpose                                    |
|--------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| PUT    | `/<filename>`               | Upload a file. Returns a plain-text URL.   |
| GET    | `/<id>/<filename>`          | Download a file (or view it in a browser). |
| POST   | `/<id>/<filename>`          | Submit the password for a protected file.  |
| GET    | `/qr/<id>/<filename>`       | PNG QR code for the download link.         |
| POST   | `/secret`                   | Store an encrypted burn-after-read secret. |
| GET    | `/secret/<id>/<key>`        | Read and destroy a secret.                 |
| POST   | `/pretty`                   | Upload JSON/YAML/XML for pretty-printing.  |
| GET    | `/pretty/<id>/<filename>`   | View the pretty-printed document.          |
| GET    | `/`                         | Landing page, or plain-text help for CLIs. |

Status codes: `200` success, `400` bad request or invalid secret key, `401`
wrong password, `404` missing, expired, or already-consumed, `411` missing
`Content-Length` on a non-chunked upload, `413` too large, `429` rate limited.

Responses to command-line clients are plain text, so they can be used directly
in scripts:

    URL=$(curl -s -T ./build.log https://qurl.sh | head -1 | awk '{print $NF}')
    echo "Build log: $URL"

---

## Privacy and retention

- No account, email address or API key is required or collected.
- Every file is deleted automatically — on download-count exhaustion, on TTL
  expiry, or by an hourly sweep, whichever comes first.
- Secrets are stored encrypted with a key the server never sees.
- Passwords are stored as salted hashes, never in plain text.
- All traffic is served over HTTPS.

Do not use qurl.sh as durable storage or as a backup destination: everything
uploaded is designed to disappear.

---

## Shell helper

A convenience function for `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`:

    qurl() {
      if [ -t 0 ] && [ -n "$1" ]; then
        curl -T "$1" https://qurl.sh
      else
        curl -T - "https://qurl.sh/${1:-stdin.txt}"
      fi
    }

Then:

    qurl ./report.pdf
    cat access.log | qurl access.log
